questions.q: When remediating the unpatched-servers finding, why does the fix start with triage by CVSS score rather than patching every server in whatever order they're listed?
options: A critical, internet-facing vulnerability needs to be closed before a low-severity issue on an isolated system, so severity and exposure drive the order
CVSS score determines which servers are Windows versus Linux
Patches should always be applied alphabetically by hostname
Triage isn't necessary once an SLA exists
questions.explain: Prioritizing by CVSS score and exposure means the highest-risk gaps close first, which is what a real patch SLA is built around.

questions.q: What's the first step in fixing the overly permissive domain-wide GPO finding?
options: Pull the actual GPO report to see exactly what it grants, rather than guessing at the misconfiguration
Immediately delete the GPO without review
Disable Group Policy processing domain-wide
Restart every domain controller
questions.explain: Get-GPOReport shows precisely what the GPO grants, which is what's needed before narrowing local Administrators membership back down.

questions.q: Why does finding 3 — root SSH login enabled on a Linux database server — get treated as a possible compromise rather than a quiet config fix?
options: Because root login with password auth exposed for an unknown length of time means someone could have used it, so the logs have to be checked before assuming it's just a misconfiguration
Because SSH misconfigurations are always treated the same as unpatched servers
Because database servers never need SSH hardening
Because root login is actually a Windows-only concept
questions.explain: An exposed root login on a database server carries real compromise risk, so the auth log and audit history get checked before the fix is considered the end of the story.

questions.q: What does "closing the loop" mean for all three findings in this case study?
options: Re-verifying and re-scanning each fix with documented proof, not just applying a change and assuming it worked
Simply informing the auditor verbally that fixes were made
Deleting the original audit report once remediation begins
Waiting for the next scheduled audit to confirm anything was fixed
questions.explain: A fix without documented re-verification is the same audit finding again next year — proof is what actually closes the loop.

questions.q: What do all three audit findings in this case study have in common, in terms of the knowledge needed to fix them?
options: None of them require new material — each maps directly to a concept already covered earlier in this course
Each one requires a brand-new tool not covered anywhere else in the course
They can only be fixed by a third-party vendor
They have nothing in common and require unrelated skill sets
questions.explain: Patch management, GPO baselines, and SSH hardening were all covered earlier in this course — the case study is about applying that material under pressure.
